newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: POSCO sees steel prices under a cloud.
newsitem.headline: POSCO sees steel prices under a cloud.

text.p: South Korea's largest steel maker Pohang Iron & Steel Co Ltd (POSCO) said on Tuesday it expected steel prices in South East Asian markets to remain under pressure for up to five years,

"When I visited (Australia's The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd) BHP yesterday, I think we all agreed that (in) the steel market in the near future - up to, say, five years - prices of steel will be very weak, low," company chairman Kim Mahn Je told reporters.
Kim, who is attending a conference in Australia targeted primarily at boosting Asian trade, said prices for some steel products had fallen up to 15 percent in 1996.
Kim's latest forecast contrasts with his prediction during a visit to Finland in September that world steel prices had bottomed and would improve in the short-term.

"The price will stay very low for quite a while for two reasons: the CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States) is still exporting a large quantity and the U.S. has added big capacities through electric arc producers and also mini mill producers," he said.
"So we don't foresee very attractive prices for this part of the world, particularly the South East Asian countries... where everybody is trying to export and prices are coming down very fast."
Kim singled out Taiwan as posing an increasing threat.

"Taiwan is adding their capacity and on and on I think Taiwan is becoming one of our competitors...because with a limited domestic market they'll be exporting almost half of their production to the outside world," he said.

Weaker prices and continuing high overheads had eroded POSCO's profitability in 1996, despite the group maintaining sales at similar levels to last year and domestic market share at around 55 percent, Kim said.

"The steel industry has a very simple cost structure...so once the price dips, say 10 percent, it really wipes out profit margins. In the case of POSCO, last year we were very lucky that we made almost 11 percent profit out of total sales. This year we expect about eight percent," he said.

The chairman said rising costs of iron ore, for which POSCO relies mostly on imports from Australia and Canada, and coal had forced the group to consider looking to alternative sources of raw materials.

"Mining companies are caught in a cost squeeze and they try to deflect some of those costs to the importers. It's tempting to create a situation where companies like POSCO and Nippon Steel diversify our sources of raw materials for cheaper sources," he said.
Kim considered Brazil, Venezuela and South Africa possible new sources of iron ore, while lower grade coal prices from China and South Africa also were attractive.

"For coal, China is a possible candidate. With lower quality, it's cheaper. You can mix a certain proportion of coal with high grade coal. And South Africa is a potential candidate for coal as well," he said.
